newsitem.title: BURUNDI: Burundi premier says boycott fuels extremism.
newsitem.headline: Burundi premier says boycott fuels extremism.

text.p: Burundi's military-appointed Prime Minister Pascal Firmin Ndimira said on Tuesday sanctions were helping extremists on both sides of the country's bloody ethnic divide.

Ndimira, appointed by Tutsi military ruler Pierre Buyoya after he took power on July 25, said regional countries which slapped the boycott on the landlocked state should immediately lift the embargo or be party to the country's collapse.
"The embargo reinforces extreme positions," Ndimira told a news conference, adding that rebels had stepped up their attacks on civilians since the embargo was imposed.

The military ruler who took over after the army deposed ethnic Hutu President Sylvestre Ntibantunganya says he wants to prevent genocide in the country, which has been rent by three years of civil war.
Saying he is more of a democrat than his rivals are, Buyoya has unbanned political parties and announced the restoration of the national assembly.
But some states in the region have said this does not go far enough. They want a return to contitutional rule and immediate talks with the rebels before the boycott can be lifted.

Ndimira said the government had offered to talk to rebels as part of its transition plan. Buyoya has said the Hutu rebels must reject the ideology of genocide and stop killing civilians, before any negotiations can start.
Officials from East African countries are expected to meet in neighbouring Rwanda on Wednesday to discuss the blockade which cut off Burundi's oil imports and exports of coffee, the main cash earner.
Ndimira said many companies in Burundi had cut back on production and sacked redundant workers, adding that the embargo had cost the country around $125 million. He did not elaborate.
Around 150,000 people, mainly civilians, have been killed in violence since a failed coup in which the country's first democratically elected president was killed in October 1993.
